concepts.def: A non-cellular infectious particle consisting of nucleic acid enclosed in a protein capsid, in some cases with an outer envelope. The few features shared by all viruses are a small, fixed size (most are tens to a few hundred nanometres across and do not grow); nucleic acid, either DNA or RNA, as genetic material; a capsid made of protein; no cytoplasm; and few or no enzymes. Because they have no metabolism of their own, viruses can only be replicated inside a living host cell.

The protein coat of a virus, built from many copies of one or a few protein subunits, that encloses and protects the viral nucleic acid. Every virus has a capsid; it is protein, not a membrane. Capsid shape varies between viruses (for example helical or icosahedral), and in a bacteriophage the icosahedral head is joined to a protein tail.

The nucleic acid that carries a virus's genes. In any one virus it is either DNA or RNA, never both, and it may be single-stranded or double-stranded. It codes for the capsid proteins and for any enzymes the virus needs that the host cell cannot supply, but it does not code for the ribosomes or energy-transferring systems that the virus takes from the host.

A virus whose capsid is surrounded by a lipid bilayer envelope derived from a membrane of the host cell, acquired as the virus buds through that membrane on leaving the cell. Viral glycoproteins inserted in the envelope bind to receptors on the surface of a new host cell. Coronaviruses and HIV are enveloped; bacteriophage lambda is not enveloped, so its capsid is its outermost layer.

A virus that infects the bacterium Escherichia coli. It has a linear double-stranded DNA genome of about 48 500 base pairs packed inside an icosahedral protein head, which is joined to a flexible protein tail through which the DNA is injected into the host. It is not enveloped. Lambda is a temperate phage: after infecting a cell it may follow either the lytic cycle or the lysogenic cycle.

A group of enveloped viruses with a single-stranded RNA genome, among the largest of any RNA virus, enclosed in a helical nucleocapsid. Club-shaped spike glycoproteins projecting from the envelope give the crown-like appearance in electron micrographs and bind to receptors on host cells. The RNA is copied by an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase and is not converted into DNA. Coronaviruses cause respiratory diseases in humans, including COVID-19.

An enveloped retrovirus with two copies of a single-stranded RNA genome inside a cone-shaped protein capsid, together with a few viral enzymes, including reverse transcriptase, integrase and protease. Glycoproteins in the envelope bind to receptors on helper T lymphocytes. After entry, reverse transcriptase copies the RNA into DNA, which is integrated into the host cell's DNA. HIV carries only these few enzymes and relies on the host cell for everything else, illustrating the general rule that viruses have few or no enzymes.

The mode of existence in which a virus can only be replicated inside a living host cell. Viruses have no ribosomes, no source of ATP and few or no enzymes, so they rely on the host cell for energy supply (ATP from the host's cell respiration), nutrition (nucleotides and amino acids), protein synthesis (host ribosomes, transfer RNA and RNA polymerase) and other life functions. Outside a cell a virus is inert.

The cycle in which a virus multiplies and destroys its host cell. In lambda the phases are: attachment, in which the tail binds to a specific receptor protein on the surface of an E. coli cell; DNA entry, in which the linear DNA is injected through the tail into the cytoplasm while the capsid stays outside, after which the DNA forms a circle; synthesis, in which host RNA polymerase transcribes the phage genes, host ribosomes translate them into phage proteins, and the phage DNA is replicated using host nucleotides and ATP; assembly, in which capsid proteins self-assemble around copies of the DNA to form new phages; and lysis, in which phage-encoded proteins break down the cell wall and membrane so the cell bursts, releasing on the order of a hundred new phages.

The cycle in which the phage DNA, instead of directing the synthesis of new phages, is inserted into the host cell's chromosome by a phage-encoded integrase enzyme and remains there as a prophage. A phage repressor protein keeps the genes for the lytic cycle switched off, so the genes for phage structural proteins and lysis are not expressed and no phage particles are made and the host cell is not harmed. The prophage is replicated along with the host chromosome at every cell division and passed to both daughter cells, so a whole population of E. coli can come to carry the phage genome.

The genome of a phage such as lambda when it is integrated into the chromosome of a bacterial host cell during the lysogenic cycle. It is part of the host's DNA, not a separate loop, and is copied by the host's DNA replication machinery whenever the chromosome is copied. A bacterium carrying a prophage is called a lysogen.

The switch of a prophage from the lysogenic cycle to the lytic cycle. In lambda it is triggered when the host's DNA is damaged, for example by ultraviolet light: the host's DNA-damage response leads to destruction of the phage repressor, the prophage DNA is excised from the chromosome, and the genes for the lytic cycle are expressed, so new phages are made and the cell lyses. Induction shows that lysogeny is a reversible state, not a separate kind of virus.

The independent evolution of similar features in unrelated lineages because they face the same selective pressures. All viruses share an extreme form of obligate parasitism, which favours a minimal particle: small, fixed size, a protective protein capsid and reliance on the host for metabolism. The features all viruses have in common could therefore have arisen separately in several lineages, so they cannot be taken as evidence that all viruses descend from one common ancestor.

The hypothesis that viruses did not arise once but on several separate occasions from cellular organisms, for example from fragments of cellular genetic material that gained the ability to move between cells, or by loss of structures from parasitic cells. Two lines of evidence support an origin from cellular organisms and several origins rather than one: viruses use the same genetic code as living organisms, which indicates that they are derived from them; and viruses are extremely diverse, with genomes of single- or double-stranded RNA or DNA and very different structures, which is hard to reconcile with descent from a single ancestral virus.

concepts.term: Reasons for rapid evolution in viruses
concepts.def: Some viruses, especially RNA viruses such as influenza viruses and HIV, evolve far faster than cellular organisms because: the enzymes that copy their genomes (RNA-dependent RNA polymerase in influenza, reverse transcriptase in HIV) lack the proofreading of DNA polymerases, so the mutation rate per base per replication is very high; generation times are short, with each infected cell releasing large numbers of new virions; the resulting enormous populations contain many variants for natural selection to act on; and the host's immune responses and antiviral drugs exert strong selection. Influenza viruses can also exchange genome segments between strains.

The gradual change in the surface antigens of influenza viruses, haemagglutinin and neuraminidase, caused by the accumulation of point mutations in the genes coding for them during error-prone replication. Variants whose antigens are no longer recognised by antibodies in the population are favoured by natural selection. Drift is why the strains circulating change from one season to the next and why the influenza vaccine is reformulated every year.

A sudden, major change in the surface antigens of influenza A viruses produced by reassortment: the genome consists of eight separate RNA segments, and when two different strains (for example a human strain and a strain from birds or pigs) infect the same cell, new virions can be assembled containing a mixture of segments from both. The new subtype has antigens to which few people have immunity, so shift is associated with pandemics, such as the 2009 H1N1 pandemic strain, which combined segments derived from swine, avian and human influenza viruses.

concepts.term: Consequences of rapid viral evolution for treatment
concepts.def: Because rapidly evolving viruses generate resistant or antigenically altered variants quickly, treatment must be designed around this. HIV is treated with a combination of several antiretroviral drugs acting on different targets (for example reverse transcriptase, protease and integrase), because resistance to any single drug arises readily by mutation but a single virion is very unlikely to carry mutations conferring resistance to all of them at once. Influenza vaccines are reformulated each year to match the antigens of the strains predicted to circulate. The antigenic diversity of HIV, which differs even between variants within one patient, is one of the reasons no effective HIV vaccine has yet been produced.

mcqs.q: Which feature is shared by all viruses?
options: A capsid of protein enclosing either DNA or RNA, but not both
A cytoplasm in which the virus carries out metabolism
A membrane of phospholipid forming the outermost layer
A genome of DNA together with RNA, as in any living cell
mcqs.specStatementText: What every virus has in common
mcqs.explain: The few features common to all viruses are a small, fixed size; nucleic acid, either DNA or RNA, as genetic material; a capsid made of protein; no cytoplasm; and few or no enzymes. No virus contains both DNA and RNA as its genetic material.
rationales: The few features common to all viruses are a small, fixed size; nucleic acid, either DNA or RNA, as genetic material; a capsid made of protein; no cytoplasm; and few or no enzymes. No virus contains both DNA and RNA as its genetic material.
A student who thinks of a virus as a very small cell picks this. Viruses have no cytoplasm and no metabolism of their own; every life function is carried out for them by the host cell.

A student who pictures the capsid as a kind of cell membrane picks this. The capsid is protein. Only enveloped viruses have a lipid layer, and it is host membrane outside the capsid, not a feature of all viruses.

A student who assumes genetic material must be DNA with RNA as a working copy picks this. A virus has one type of nucleic acid, DNA or RNA, never both; many viruses have RNA as their only nucleic acid.

mcqs.q: A newly discovered particle 30 nm across contains one molecule of single-stranded RNA inside a protein shell. It has no ribosomes and it multiplies only inside living cells. How does the particle multiply?
options: It grows to about twice its size inside the cell and then divides into two identical particles.
Its RNA and proteins are made by the host cell's machinery and then assembled into new particles.
It absorbs nutrients from the cell into its cytoplasm and metabolizes them to build copies of itself.
It must first acquire a DNA molecule, because one RNA strand cannot act as genetic material.
mcqs.specStatementText: What every virus has in common
mcqs.explain: The particle has the features of a virus: fixed size, one nucleic acid, a protein capsid, no cytoplasm. With no ribosomes or metabolism it relies on the host for energy, nutrition and protein synthesis, and new particles are assembled from the components the host makes.
rationales: A student who transfers binary fission from bacteria to viruses picks this. Viruses have a small, fixed size: they do not grow and do not divide. New particles are assembled at full size from separately made components.

The particle has the features of a virus: fixed size, one nucleic acid, a protein capsid, no cytoplasm. With no ribosomes or metabolism it relies on the host for energy, nutrition and protein synthesis, and new particles are assembled from the components the host makes.

A student who thinks of the particle as a tiny cell picks this. It has no cytoplasm and, with no ribosomes and few or no enzymes, no metabolism; the host cell's cytoplasm is where the copying and protein synthesis happen.

A student who believes genetic material has to be DNA picks this. Nucleic acid of either type can be a viral genome; single-stranded RNA is the genetic material of coronaviruses and of HIV, and needs no DNA partner to be a genome.

mcqs.q: Which is a correct comparison of bacteriophage lambda and HIV?
options: Both have an icosahedral head joined to a tail through which the genetic material is injected.
Both carry reverse transcriptase so that their genetic material can be copied into DNA.
Lambda has double-stranded DNA and no envelope, whereas HIV has RNA and an envelope.
Both have a capsid made of phospholipid taken from the membrane of the host cell.
mcqs.specStatementText: Viruses differ widely in shape, genome and envelope
mcqs.explain: Lambda is a non-enveloped phage with a double-stranded DNA genome in a head-and-tail capsid. HIV is an enveloped retrovirus with two single-stranded RNA molecules. The two illustrate the diversity of viral genetic material and structure.
rationales: A student whose model of every virus is the bacteriophage diagram picks this. Only phages have a tail; HIV is an enveloped particle with a cone-shaped capsid that enters the cell by fusion of its envelope with the membrane.

A student who generalises HIV's mechanism to all viruses picks this. Reverse transcriptase is a feature of retroviruses; lambda already has a DNA genome, which is transcribed and replicated by host enzymes.

Lambda is a non-enveloped phage with a double-stranded DNA genome in a head-and-tail capsid. HIV is an enveloped retrovirus with two single-stranded RNA molecules. The two illustrate the diversity of viral genetic material and structure.
A student who confuses the capsid with a membrane picks this. The capsid of every virus is protein. HIV has a host-derived lipid envelope outside its protein capsid; lambda has no lipid at all.

mcqs.q: A newly isolated virus is inactivated by detergents that dissolve lipid bilayers, whereas bacteriophage lambda is unaffected by the same detergents. What does this indicate about the structure of the new virus?
options: It has a lipid envelope that it synthesized itself, using enzymes encoded in its own genome.
Its capsid is itself a phospholipid membrane, so the detergent dissolves the coat around its nucleic acid.
It is a tiny cell whose plasma membrane, enclosing its cytoplasm, is destroyed by the detergent.
It is enveloped in host cell membrane, a lipid bilayer lying outside its protein capsid.
mcqs.specStatementText: Viruses differ widely in shape, genome and envelope
mcqs.explain: Sensitivity to lipid-dissolving detergents shows the particle depends on a lipid bilayer. Viruses do not make lipid; the envelope is host cell membrane acquired as the virus leaves the cell, carrying viral glycoproteins that bind the next host. Lambda is not enveloped, so its protein capsid is its outermost layer and detergents do not inactivate it.
rationales: A student who assumes every part of a virus is made from viral genes picks this. The lipid is correctly identified, but a virus has no metabolism and no enzymes for lipid synthesis; the envelope is a section of host cell membrane taken as the virus buds out of the cell.

A student who thinks the capsid is a lipid membrane picks this. The capsid of every virus, including this one, is a protein shell. What the detergent dissolves is a separate lipid envelope outside the capsid, present only in enveloped viruses; lambda has no lipid layer, so it is unaffected.

A student who thinks a virus is a small cell picks this. A virus has no cytoplasm and no membrane of its own; the lipid the detergent attacks is borrowed host membrane wrapped around a protein capsid.

Sensitivity to lipid-dissolving detergents shows the particle depends on a lipid bilayer. Viruses do not make lipid; the envelope is host cell membrane acquired as the virus leaves the cell, carrying viral glycoproteins that bind the next host. Lambda is not enveloped, so its protein capsid is its outermost layer and detergents do not inactivate it.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the genetic material of viruses is correct?
options: It is DNA or RNA, and either type may be single-stranded or double-stranded.
It is DNA in every virus, with RNA also present, as in a living cell.
It is RNA in every virus, and is copied into DNA by reverse transcriptase.
It is double-stranded DNA in every virus, as it is in bacteriophage lambda.
mcqs.specStatementText: Viruses differ widely in shape, genome and envelope
mcqs.explain: Viral genomes are highly diverse: double-stranded DNA in bacteriophage lambda, single-stranded RNA in coronaviruses and HIV, and single-stranded DNA or double-stranded RNA in other groups. Each virus has one type of nucleic acid.
rationales: Viral genomes are highly diverse: double-stranded DNA in bacteriophage lambda, single-stranded RNA in coronaviruses and HIV, and single-stranded DNA or double-stranded RNA in other groups. Each virus has one type of nucleic acid.
A student who assumes the cellular pattern of DNA genome plus RNA copies applies to viruses picks this. Many viruses have only RNA, and no virus has both DNA and RNA as its genetic material.
A student who generalises from HIV picks this. Only retroviruses use reverse transcriptase; coronaviruses copy RNA directly to RNA, and lambda and many other viruses have DNA genomes.
A student who takes the phage as the model for all viruses picks this. Lambda does have double-stranded DNA, but coronaviruses and HIV have single-stranded RNA genomes.

mcqs.q: In the lytic cycle of bacteriophage lambda, what happens after the phage has attached to a receptor on the surface of an E. coli cell?
options: The whole phage is taken into the cell and the capsid is broken down in the cytoplasm.
The phage DNA passes through the tail into the cell, and the capsid remains outside it.
The phage membrane fuses with the bacterial membrane, releasing the DNA inside.
The phage releases its ribosomes and enzymes into the cell to begin making phage proteins.
mcqs.specStatementText: The lytic cycle: the host cell does the work, then bursts
mcqs.explain: After attachment, lambda injects its DNA through the tail into the cytoplasm. The head and tail remain outside the cell wall. Only the DNA is needed inside, because the host cell provides everything else for synthesis of new phages.
rationales: A student who applies the entry of animal viruses to phages picks this. A phage cannot cross the bacterial cell wall; the capsid stays on the outside and only the DNA enters.

After attachment, lambda injects its DNA through the tail into the cytoplasm. The head and tail remain outside the cell wall. Only the DNA is needed inside, because the host cell provides everything else for synthesis of new phages.
A student who thinks the outer coat of a phage is a membrane picks this. Lambda has no lipid membrane: its outer layer is a protein capsid, and it delivers its DNA by injection through the tail.

A student who thinks the virus brings its own synthetic machinery picks this. Lambda has no ribosomes; phage proteins are made by the host's ribosomes after host RNA polymerase transcribes the phage DNA.

mcqs.q: A single lambda phage infects an E. coli cell in a large culture. Each lytic cycle takes 40 minutes and ends with lysis releasing 100 phages, every one of which immediately infects a fresh cell. How many phages are released by the lysis events that occur 120 minutes after the first infection?
mcqs.specStatementText: The lytic cycle: the host cell does the work, then bursts
mcqs.explain: Lysis at 40 minutes releases 100 phages, which infect 100 cells; lysis at 80 minutes releases 100 × 100 = 10⁴ phages, which infect 10⁴ cells; lysis at 120 minutes releases 10⁴ × 100 = 1 × 10⁶ phages. Each cycle multiplies the number by the burst size.
rationales: A student who adds 100 phages for each of the three cycles picks this. Every phage released infects a new cell, so the number is multiplied by 100 in each cycle, not increased by 100.

A student who pictures the original infected cell as the only source of phages, releasing one batch of 100 at each lysis, picks this. Every released phage infects a fresh cell, so each cycle multiplies the number by 100.

Lysis at 40 minutes releases 100 phages, which infect 100 cells; lysis at 80 minutes releases 100 × 100 = 10⁴ phages, which infect 10⁴ cells; lysis at 120 minutes releases 10⁴ × 100 = 1 × 10⁶ phages. Each cycle multiplies the number by the burst size.

A student who stops after two cycles, or who counts the lysis at 120 minutes as the second rather than the third, picks this. Lysis events occur at 40, 80 and 120 minutes, so three rounds of ×100 give 1 × 10⁶.

mcqs.q: Bacteriophage lambda does not multiply in a sterile nutrient broth containing amino acids, nucleotides and ATP, but does multiply when living E. coli cells are added to the broth. Which explanation is correct?
options: The phage's own enzymes and ribosomes work only once they are activated inside a cell's cytoplasm.
The phage cannot absorb dissolved nutrients from the broth, but it can feed on the contents of a cell.
The phage has to attach to a cell wall before it can grow large enough to divide in two.
The phage lacks ribosomes and most enzymes, so it needs a cell's protein synthesis machinery.
mcqs.specStatementText: The lytic cycle: the host cell does the work, then bursts
mcqs.explain: Raw materials and ATP are not enough. A virus has no ribosomes, transfer RNA or RNA polymerase and few or no enzymes, so its DNA can only be transcribed, translated and replicated inside a cell that supplies these. This is the obligate parasitism the IB describes.
rationales: A student who thinks the virus carries its own synthetic machinery picks this. Lambda has no ribosomes and very few enzymes to activate; the machinery that makes phage proteins belongs to the host.

A student who treats the phage as a tiny cell that feeds picks this. A virus does not absorb or metabolize nutrients at all; the host cell's own metabolism does the work using the phage's genetic instructions.
A student who thinks viruses reproduce by growth and division picks this. Phages have a fixed size and do not divide; new phages are assembled from proteins and DNA made inside the host cell.

Raw materials and ATP are not enough. A virus has no ribosomes, transfer RNA or RNA polymerase and few or no enzymes, so its DNA can only be transcribed, translated and replicated inside a cell that supplies these. This is the obligate parasitism the IB describes.

mcqs.q: What happens to the DNA of bacteriophage lambda in the lysogenic cycle?
options: It is integrated into the host chromosome and is copied along with it.
It stays as a separate circle in the cytoplasm, like a plasmid, replicating on its own.
It is transcribed slowly, making a few phages that leave the cell without lysis.
It is permanently inactivated, so the cell and its descendants can no longer make phages.
mcqs.specStatementText: The lysogenic cycle: the phage genome hides in the host chromosome
mcqs.explain: In lysogeny the lambda DNA is integrated into the E. coli chromosome as a prophage. It is replicated with the chromosome at each cell division and inherited by both daughter cells, while the genes for the lytic cycle are kept switched off.
rationales: In lysogeny the lambda DNA is integrated into the E. coli chromosome as a prophage. It is replicated with the chromosome at each cell division and inherited by both daughter cells, while the genes for the lytic cycle are kept switched off.

A student who files any extra circle of DNA in a bacterium as a plasmid picks this. The lambda prophage is integrated into the chromosome by integrase and is copied only when the chromosome is copied.

A student who imagines lysogeny as a slow lytic cycle picks this. No phages are produced during lysogeny: a repressor keeps the lytic genes off, and phages are only made after induction, when the cell lyses.

A student who thinks a prophage is a dead end picks this. The prophage remains intact and can be induced, for example by ultraviolet damage to the host DNA, to leave the chromosome and enter the lytic cycle.

mcqs.q: A culture of E. coli cells carrying the lambda prophage is growing normally. It is exposed to ultraviolet light, and about an hour later most of the cells lyse and release phages. Which explanation is correct?
options: The prophage had been releasing phages all along, and the ultraviolet light merely burst the cells.
Damage to the host DNA induced the prophage to be excised from the chromosome and enter the lytic cycle.
A prophage cannot cause lysis, so the culture must have been contaminated by a separate lytic phage.
The ultraviolet light made the prophage grow and divide repeatedly until the cells burst.
mcqs.specStatementText: The lysogenic cycle: the phage genome hides in the host chromosome
mcqs.explain: Ultraviolet light damages DNA, and the host's damage response leads to destruction of the phage repressor. The prophage is excised, the lytic genes are expressed, new phages are assembled and the cells lyse. This is induction, the switch from the lysogenic to the lytic cycle.
rationales: A student who thinks lysogeny involves slow phage production picks this. A prophage produces no phages; the culture had been growing normally with none released, and the phages appeared only after induction.

Ultraviolet light damages DNA, and the host's damage response leads to destruction of the phage repressor. The prophage is excised, the lytic genes are expressed, new phages are assembled and the cells lyse. This is induction, the switch from the lysogenic to the lytic cycle.

A student who treats lytic and lysogenic as two fixed kinds of phage picks this. Lambda is a temperate phage: the same prophage that was dormant can be induced into the lytic cycle, so no second phage is needed.

A student who thinks viruses multiply by growth and division picks this. The prophage does not grow; after induction the phage DNA is replicated and phage proteins are made by the host, and complete phages are assembled before lysis.

mcqs.q: All viruses are very small, have a protein capsid and depend completely on a host cell. How do biologists interpret these shared features?
options: As homologous features that all viruses have inherited from a single ancestral virus.
As ancestral features retained from the first living things, from which cells later evolved.
As convergent evolution: extreme obligate parasitism imposes the same demands on unrelated viruses.
As the features of the smallest possible cells, reduced to nothing except their most essential parts.
mcqs.specStatementText: Viruses probably arose several times from cellular life
mcqs.explain: Every virus lives by an extreme form of obligate parasitism, which selects for a minimal particle that can protect its genome and get it into a cell. Features shared for this reason could have arisen independently in several lineages, so they are not evidence of a single origin.
rationales: A student who applies the rule 'shared features imply common ancestry' without considering convergence picks this. The IB states that the structural features viruses have in common could be regarded as convergent evolution, not homology.

A student who equates simplicity with antiquity picks this. Viruses depend entirely on cells and share the genetic code with them, so they are derived from cellular organisms; their simplicity is a result of parasitism.

Every virus lives by an extreme form of obligate parasitism, which selects for a minimal particle that can protect its genome and get it into a cell. Features shared for this reason could have arisen independently in several lineages, so they are not evidence of a single origin.

A student who thinks of viruses as tiny cells picks this. Viruses are not cells: they have no cytoplasm, no ribosomes and no metabolism, which is why they are described as particles rather than as reduced cells.

mcqs.q: Viruses use the same genetic code as cellular organisms, yet their genomes may be single- or double-stranded RNA or DNA, whereas all cells have double-stranded DNA genomes. Which conclusion is consistent with both observations?
options: Viruses all descend from one ancestral virus, just as all cells descend from a single common ancestor.
Viruses evolved before cells existed, and cells later inherited the genetic code from them.
Viruses with RNA genomes must convert them into double-stranded DNA before the code can be used.
Viruses are derived from cellular organisms, and probably arose on several separate occasions.
mcqs.specStatementText: Viruses probably arose several times from cellular life
mcqs.explain: The shared genetic code indicates that viruses are derived from living organisms rather than having an independent origin. The diversity of their genomes and structures is hard to reconcile with a single ancestral virus, so the IB describes the evidence as suggesting several possible origins.
rationales: A student who assumes every group must have a single root picks this. The shared code links viruses to cells, not to each other, and the diversity of genome types points away from a single ancestral virus.

A student who treats the simplest replicator as the oldest picks this. Viruses are obligate parasites with no metabolism, so they could not have existed before the cells they depend on; the evidence is for origins of viruses from other organisms.

A student who generalises HIV's reverse transcription to all RNA viruses picks this. Coronavirus RNA is translated directly by host ribosomes using the same code; no conversion to DNA is needed, and this says nothing about origins.

The shared genetic code indicates that viruses are derived from living organisms rather than having an independent origin. The diversity of their genomes and structures is hard to reconcile with a single ancestral virus, so the IB describes the evidence as suggesting several possible origins.

mcqs.q: Why do influenza viruses and HIV evolve so rapidly?
options: Their genome-copying enzymes lack proofreading, and vast numbers of virions are produced quickly.
Their RNA genomes are chemically unstable, so bases change spontaneously between one infection and the next.
They alter their genes deliberately whenever they are attacked by antibodies or by antiviral drugs.
They divide in two every few minutes, as bacteria do, so mutations accumulate over many divisions.
mcqs.specStatementText: Why some viruses evolve so fast, and what that means for treatment
mcqs.explain: The RNA-dependent RNA polymerase of influenza and the reverse transcriptase of HIV do not proofread, so the mutation rate is very high. Short generation times and huge populations supply many variants, and immune responses and drugs select among them.
rationales: The RNA-dependent RNA polymerase of influenza and the reverse transcriptase of HIV do not proofread, so the mutation rate is very high. Short generation times and huge populations supply many variants, and immune responses and drugs select among them.

A student who links the short life of RNA with mutation picks this. Mutations are copying errors made during replication by enzymes without proofreading, not spontaneous changes to a genome sitting inside a virion.
A student who reads 'the virus adapts' as intention picks this. Mutations are random and occur regardless of any threat; antibodies and drugs then select the variants that happen to survive.

A student who transfers binary fission to viruses picks this. Viruses do not divide; each infected cell releases many assembled virions, and the mutations arise when the genome is copied by error-prone viral enzymes.

mcqs.q: Why must the influenza vaccine be reformulated with different strains every year, when the measles vaccine has stayed effective for decades?
options: Memory cells against influenza die within a year, so a new vaccine is needed to replace them.
Point mutations change influenza's surface antigens each year, so earlier antibodies no longer bind to them.
Reassortment of the genome segments produces a completely new influenza subtype every year.
The influenza virus mutates in response to the vaccine so that it can escape the antibodies produced.
mcqs.specStatementText: Why some viruses evolve so fast, and what that means for treatment
mcqs.explain: Antigenic drift, the accumulation of point mutations in the haemagglutinin and neuraminidase genes, alters the antigens of circulating strains. Antibodies and memory cells raised against last year's strains fail to recognise the new ones, so the vaccine is changed to match. Measles virus antigens have barely changed.
rationales: A student who thinks the jab simply 'wears off' picks this. Memory cells persist for years; the problem is that the virus has changed, which is why the vaccine must be reformulated rather than merely repeated.

Antigenic drift, the accumulation of point mutations in the haemagglutinin and neuraminidase genes, alters the antigens of circulating strains. Antibodies and memory cells raised against last year's strains fail to recognise the new ones, so the vaccine is changed to match. Measles virus antigens have barely changed.

A student who confuses antigenic shift with drift picks this. Reassortment between strains in a co-infected cell is rare and produces pandemic subtypes occasionally; the annual changes are due to point mutations.

A student who thinks the virus changes on purpose picks this. Mutations arise at random during error-prone replication; vaccination only selects, from the variants already present, those that antibodies fail to bind.

mcqs.q: HIV infection is treated with a combination of three antiretroviral drugs that act on different viral enzymes, rather than with a single drug. Why is a combination used?
options: One drug would eliminate the virus if it were taken for long enough; three are used only to shorten the course of treatment.
HIV carries its own enzymes for every step of its replication, so all of them have to be blocked at the same time.
Resistance to one drug arises readily in the rapidly mutating population, but one virion is unlikely to resist all three.
Each drug makes HIV mutate, and three drugs together cause so many mutations that the virus is destroyed.
mcqs.specStatementText: Why some viruses evolve so fast, and what that means for treatment
mcqs.explain: HIV's reverse transcriptase is error-prone and the virus population in a patient is enormous, so virions resistant to any single drug appear and are selected. Simultaneous resistance to three drugs with different targets would need several independent mutations in one virion, which is far less likely, so the combination keeps the virus suppressed.
rationales: A student who models antiviral treatment on a course of antibiotics picks this. A single drug fails because resistant variants survive and multiply; the combination is needed to prevent resistance, not to save time.

A student who thinks the virus is self-sufficient in enzymes picks this. HIV carries only a few enzymes and uses host machinery for most steps; blocking any one viral enzyme stops replication of sensitive virions. The combination is about resistance, not completeness.

HIV's reverse transcriptase is error-prone and the virus population in a patient is enormous, so virions resistant to any single drug appear and are selected. Simultaneous resistance to three drugs with different targets would need several independent mutations in one virion, which is far less likely, so the combination keeps the virus suppressed.

A student who thinks drugs cause the mutations picks this. Mutations arise at random during replication whether or not a drug is present; the drugs select among variants, and the combination works by making a fully resistant variant improbable.

mcqs.q: In 2009 a new strain of influenza A appeared with genome segments derived from swine, avian and human influenza viruses, and it caused a pandemic. Which process produced this strain?
options: Gradual accumulation of point mutations in the haemagglutinin gene of one strain.
Reverse transcription of the viral RNA followed by insertion of host genes.
Mutation of the virus in response to widespread vaccination against the earlier strains.
Reassortment of RNA genome segments in a cell infected by two different strains.
mcqs.specStatementText: Why some viruses evolve so fast, and what that means for treatment
mcqs.explain: The influenza A genome is in eight separate RNA segments. When two strains infect the same cell, new virions can be assembled with segments from both, producing antigenic shift: a novel subtype to which few people have immunity, which is why it spread as a pandemic.
rationales: A student who runs antigenic drift and shift together picks this. Point mutations alter existing antigens gradually; they cannot bring whole genome segments from swine and avian viruses into a human strain.

A student who generalises HIV's mechanism to all RNA viruses picks this. Influenza has no reverse transcriptase and no DNA stage; its new segments came from other influenza strains, not from host genes.

A student who thinks viruses change purposefully picks this. Vaccination does not cause genetic change, and no mutation can copy segments from other viruses; the strain arose by reassortment in a co-infected cell.
